questions.q: An owner uses a building she could rent to another business for $2,000 per month. In economic-cost analysis, the forgone rent is:
options: An implicit cost
An explicit cost
Accounting revenue
A sunk cost
questions.feedback: Using an owner-supplied resource sacrifices its next-best return, so the forgone rent is an implicit cost.

questions.q: Which cost is explicit for a small restaurant?
options: The owner’s forgone salary at another job
The interest the owner could have earned on invested savings
The rent the owner could earn from an owned building
The monthly payment to its food supplier
questions.feedback: An explicit cost is a direct monetary payment made by the firm.

questions.q: Economic cost includes:
options: Only payments that vary with output
Only costs paid in cash this month
Both explicit payments and implicit opportunity costs
Only costs recorded by an accountant
questions.feedback: Economic cost counts both recorded payments and the value of forgone alternatives.

questions.q: A photographer quits a $48,000 salaried job to operate a studio she owns. She makes no wage payment to herself. The $48,000 is best treated as:
options: Revenue earned by the studio
An implicit cost of operating the studio
An explicit labor expense
A sunk cost from the former job
questions.feedback: The salary sacrificed by using the owner’s labor in the business is an opportunity cost.

questions.q: A business uses $100,000 of the owner’s savings that could earn 5% elsewhere. Which amount belongs in economic cost because of that choice?
options: $5,000 of forgone investment income
$100,000 of explicit interest expense
$105,000 of accounting cost
$0 because the firm borrowed nothing
questions.feedback: The relevant implicit cost is the return sacrificed on the owner’s capital: 5% of $100,000.

questions.q: A firm rents one warehouse for $30,000 and uses a second warehouse owned by the proprietor that could rent for $24,000. Which statement is correct?
options: Both amounts are explicit
Both amounts are implicit
Only the $24,000 belongs in economic cost
The $30,000 is explicit and the $24,000 is implicit
questions.feedback: The rental payment is explicit; forgone rent on owner-owned property is an implicit opportunity cost.

questions.q: A contractor owns a truck that could be leased to another firm for $9,000 a year. If the truck is used in the contractor’s own business, the $9,000 is:
options: A fixed accounting payment to the owner
Irrelevant because no cash changes hands
Part of the business’s economic cost
An accounting expense only if the truck is sold
questions.feedback: The forgone lease income is the opportunity cost of using the truck internally.

questions.q: Recorded expenses are $70,000. The owner also gives up a $40,000 salary and $5,000 of interest. Total economic cost is:
questions.feedback: Economic cost equals explicit cost plus all implicit opportunity costs: $70,000 + $40,000 + $5,000.

questions.q: Two otherwise identical businesses each pay $80,000 in recorded expenses. Owner A gives up a $50,000 salary; Owner B gives up a $35,000 salary and $20,000 of investment income. Which has the higher economic cost?
options: Owner B’s business by $5,000
Owner A’s business by $5,000
They have the same economic cost
It cannot be determined without revenue
questions.feedback: A has $130,000 of economic cost; B has $135,000 because both forgone salary and forgone investment income count.

questions.q: A learner says, “If the owner did not write a check, the resource has no cost.” What is the repair?
options: Only variable resources have economic costs
Every implicit cost must appear on an invoice
Opportunity cost matters only for consumers
Owner-supplied resources can have implicit opportunity costs even without a cash payment
questions.feedback: Economic cost includes the value of the next-best use of owner-supplied resources.

questions.q: How does the general idea of opportunity cost carry into a firm’s production-cost analysis?
options: Opportunity cost is replaced by accounting profit
A firm counts only costs that change with output
Resources supplied by the owner are valued by the best alternative return sacrificed
Only purchased inputs have opportunity cost
questions.feedback: The same next-best-alternative principle applies to labor, capital, land, and other resources used by a firm.

questions.q: A firm has $150,000 in revenue and $110,000 in explicit costs. Its accounting profit is:
questions.feedback: Accounting profit equals revenue minus explicit costs.

questions.q: Economic profit is calculated as:
options: Revenue minus explicit and implicit costs
Revenue minus explicit costs only
Accounting profit plus implicit costs
Revenue minus fixed cost only
questions.feedback: Economic profit subtracts all opportunity costs, including implicit costs.

questions.q: Normal profit is best understood as:
options: A guaranteed positive economic profit
Revenue remaining after variable cost only
A payment excluded from economic cost
The return needed to keep owner-supplied resources in their current use
questions.feedback: Normal profit is part of implicit cost and represents the opportunity cost of entrepreneurial resources.

questions.q: If accounting profit is $60,000 and implicit costs are $25,000, economic profit is:
questions.feedback: Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs.

questions.q: A firm earning zero economic profit is:
options: Producing with zero revenue
Covering both explicit and implicit opportunity costs
Failing to cover explicit costs
Necessarily earning zero accounting profit
questions.feedback: Zero economic profit includes normal compensation for owner resources.

questions.q: A firm can have positive accounting profit but negative economic profit when:
options: Implicit opportunity costs exceed accounting profit
Explicit costs are zero
Revenue exceeds all explicit and implicit costs
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
questions.feedback: Accounting profit can look positive even though the owner would earn more in the next-best alternative.

questions.q: Positive economic profit means the firm’s revenue is:
options: Greater than explicit costs but below implicit costs
Exactly equal to total opportunity cost
Less than accounting cost
Greater than all explicit and implicit costs
questions.feedback: Positive economic profit is the return above all opportunity costs.

questions.q: A proprietor reports $95,000 of accounting profit. She gives up a $65,000 salary and $18,000 of interest by operating the business. What is her economic profit?
questions.feedback: Subtract both implicit costs from accounting profit: $95,000 − $65,000 − $18,000.

questions.q: Firm A earns $70,000 accounting profit and has $20,000 implicit cost. Firm B earns $90,000 accounting profit and has $50,000 implicit cost. Which has the larger economic profit?
options: Firm B by $20,000
Firm A by $10,000
Firm B by $10,000
They are equal
questions.feedback: Firm A earns $50,000 economic profit; Firm B earns $40,000.

questions.q: An owner could earn $75,000 elsewhere and could earn $10,000 interest on invested capital. The firm’s accounting profit is $85,000. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns zero economic profit
The firm earns $85,000 economic profit
The firm loses $10,000 accounting profit
Normal profit must be zero
questions.feedback: The $85,000 accounting profit exactly covers the $85,000 of implicit opportunity costs.

questions.q: A firm’s revenue rises by $20,000 while explicit costs rise by $8,000 and implicit costs rise by $5,000. Compared with before, economic profit changes by:
options: An increase of $12,000
An increase of $15,000
A decrease of $7,000
An increase of $7,000
questions.feedback: Economic profit changes by the revenue change minus both cost changes: $20,000 − $8,000 − $5,000.

questions.q: A learner subtracts the owner’s forgone salary when calculating accounting profit. What is the repair?
options: The forgone salary should be added to revenue
Accounting profit ignores explicit costs
Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs; the forgone salary is implicit
Accounting profit subtracts all opportunity costs
questions.feedback: Implicit costs matter for economic profit, not the accounting-profit calculation.

questions.q: A learner says economic profit equals accounting profit plus implicit costs. What is the repair?
options: Economic profit and accounting profit are always equal
Economic profit equals accounting profit minus implicit costs
Economic profit equals accounting profit plus explicit costs
Economic profit ignores owner opportunity costs
questions.feedback: Implicit costs reduce economic profit relative to accounting profit.

questions.q: A learner calls zero economic profit a “loss.” What is the repair?
options: Zero economic profit means all explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit, are covered
Zero economic profit means revenue is zero
Zero economic profit means explicit costs exceed revenue
Zero economic profit excludes owner compensation
questions.feedback: Normal profit is included in economic cost, so zero economic profit can be a sustainable outcome.

questions.q: A learner finds accounting profit of $50,000 and implicit cost of $70,000, then reports economic profit of $20,000. What is the repair?
options: $20,000 is correct because profit cannot be negative
Economic profit is $120,000
Implicit cost should be ignored
Economic profit is −$20,000
questions.feedback: Economic profit equals $50,000 − $70,000 = −$20,000.

questions.q: How does opportunity cost explain the difference between accounting profit and economic profit?
options: Economic profit ignores explicit expenses
The two measures differ only when fixed cost changes
Economic profit subtracts the forgone returns of owner-supplied resources
Accounting profit subtracts more opportunity costs than economic profit
questions.feedback: Economic profit extends accounting profit by charging the firm for owner resources at their next-best use.

questions.q: Why is normal profit connected to the idea of opportunity cost?
options: It is identical to producer surplus
It compensates entrepreneurial resources for what they could earn in their next-best use
It is a tax on accounting profit
It measures consumer willingness to pay
questions.feedback: Normal profit is the implicit opportunity cost required to keep entrepreneurial resources in the firm.

questions.q: How does marginal decision-making differ from comparing total economic profit?
options: Marginal analysis focuses on changes from one more action, while economic profit compares total revenue with all opportunity costs
Marginal analysis ignores costs entirely
Economic profit uses only marginal cost
Both calculations always use the same denominator
questions.feedback: The two tools answer different questions: one about incremental choices and one about overall return after opportunity costs.

questions.q: How does marginal product connect the production function to marginal cost when the wage is unchanged?
options: A higher marginal product necessarily raises marginal cost
Marginal product determines fixed cost
Marginal cost and marginal product move together in the same direction
A higher marginal product generally means a lower marginal cost of additional output
questions.feedback: When each worker adds more output for the same wage, the labor cost per additional unit falls.

questions.q: Why does diminishing marginal product help explain the upward-sloping portion of short-run marginal cost?
options: Total product must fall as soon as diminishing returns begin
Average fixed cost becomes negative
Additional variable input eventually adds less output, so each extra unit of output becomes more costly
Fixed cost rises with every worker
questions.feedback: With a fixed input, falling marginal product raises the variable-input cost of producing additional output.

questions.q: How does average product connect to average variable cost when labor is the only variable input and the wage is constant?
options: Average product equals total fixed cost per worker
Higher average product tends to imply lower average variable cost
Higher average product raises average fixed cost
Average product and average variable cost are unrelated
questions.feedback: More output per worker spreads the wage cost across more units of output.

questions.q: Why does the short-run/long-run distinction matter when interpreting cost curves?
options: Some inputs are fixed in the short run, while all inputs can vary in the long run
All costs are variable in both horizons
The long run is always exactly one year
Fixed costs rise only in the long run
questions.feedback: Short-run cost curves reflect at least one fixed input; long-run cost analysis allows plant size and all other inputs to change.

questions.q: How does the marginal-versus-average rule connect product curves to cost curves?
options: Marginal and average values always move in opposite directions
A marginal below an average always raises the average
The rule applies to product but never to cost
A marginal value above an average pulls the average up; a marginal cost below an average cost pulls that average down
questions.feedback: The same arithmetic relationship governs MP versus AP and MC versus AVC or ATC.

questions.q: How does identifying fixed and variable inputs help classify short-run costs?
options: Fixed inputs create marginal revenue
Variable inputs determine accounting profit but not cost
Payments tied to fixed inputs generate fixed cost, while costs of variable inputs change with output
Every input creates only variable cost
questions.feedback: Input flexibility is the production-side basis for distinguishing fixed and variable cost.

questions.q: In the short run, total fixed cost generally:
options: Falls to zero whenever output is positive
Does not change when output changes
Rises one-for-one with output
Equals marginal cost
questions.feedback: Fixed cost is tied to inputs that cannot be adjusted in the short run.

questions.q: At zero output, total variable cost is typically:
options: Zero
Equal to total fixed cost
At its maximum
Equal to average total cost
questions.feedback: Variable cost is generated by producing output, so it is zero when output is zero in the standard cost model.

questions.q: A workshop has $150 of fixed cost and $90 of variable cost at its current output. Its total cost is:
questions.feedback: Total cost combines fixed and variable cost: $150 + $90 = $240.

questions.q: If total cost is $900 and total variable cost is $650, total fixed cost is:
A firm’s TFC is $120. At an output of 8 units, TVC is $280. TC is:
A cost schedule shows TC of $510 at 5 units and TFC of $150. TVC at 5 units is:
A firm’s TC is $200 at zero output and $470 at 6 units. What is TFC?
questions.feedback: At zero output, TVC is zero, so TC equals TFC.

questions.q: A learner writes TC = TFC − TVC. What is the repair?
options: TC = MC + AFC
TC = revenue − profit
TC = TFC + TVC
TC = TVC − TFC
questions.feedback: Total cost combines the fixed and variable components.

questions.q: A learner says fixed cost must fall when output falls. What is the repair?
options: Fixed cost is another name for marginal cost
Within the short run, total fixed cost does not vary with output
Fixed cost moves one-for-one with output
Fixed cost equals zero below capacity
questions.feedback: A fixed input creates a cost that remains even as current output changes.

questions.q: A learner reports positive TVC when output is zero in the standard short-run schedule. What is the repair?
options: At zero output, TVC is zero; any remaining cost is fixed
TVC equals TFC at zero output
TVC is always greater than TC
TVC is an implicit cost only
questions.feedback: Variable costs arise from producing output, while fixed costs remain at zero output.

questions.q: A row has TFC = $90 and TC = $250, but a learner records TVC = $340. What is the repair?
options: TVC is $250
TVC is $90
TVC is $340
TVC is $160
questions.feedback: TVC = TC − TFC = $250 − $90.

questions.q: How does a fixed input in the production model connect to fixed cost?
options: Fixed inputs determine revenue rather than cost
A fixed input makes marginal cost zero
A payment associated with an input that cannot be changed in the short run contributes to fixed cost
Every fixed input creates variable cost only
questions.feedback: The production distinction between fixed and variable inputs carries directly into short-run cost classification.

questions.q: How does hiring additional labor connect production decisions to variable cost?
options: Variable cost falls automatically whenever workers are added
If labor is variable, more labor raises total variable cost
Hiring labor changes total fixed cost only
Labor cost is sunk by definition
questions.feedback: Payments to adjustable inputs are part of total variable cost.

questions.q: Why is the vertical distance between TC and TVC constant in a standard short-run total-cost graph?
options: The distance equals TFC, which does not vary with output
The distance equals MC, which is constant
TVC and TC have different output units
The distance equals profit
questions.feedback: Because TC = TFC + TVC, the fixed-cost amount separates the two curves at every output.

questions.q: How does a cost schedule support marginal analysis?
options: A cost schedule eliminates the need to compare changes
Only TFC is needed to calculate marginal cost
Marginal cost is found by adding TC and TVC
Changes in TC or TVC between output levels can be used to calculate marginal cost
questions.feedback: Cost schedules provide the change in cost associated with a change in output.

questions.q: How does TC = TFC + TVC help interpret average total cost later?
options: It implies ATC equals TFC at every output
It makes AVC independent of variable cost
Dividing each component by output gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by output gives MC = AFC + AVC
questions.feedback: The total-cost identity becomes the average-cost identity after dividing by quantity.

questions.q: Why does a pure increase in TFC leave the change in total cost between two output levels unchanged?
options: The increase reduces TVC by the same amount
The same fixed amount is added to TC at both output levels
TFC becomes variable after the increase
MC is defined as total fixed cost per unit
questions.feedback: Marginal cost depends on cost differences across output, so a constant fixed-cost addition cancels out.

questions.q: Which expression gives a firm’s fixed cost per unit of output?
options: TFC divided by Q
TVC divided by Q
Change in TC divided by change in Q
TC divided by TVC
questions.feedback: Average fixed cost spreads total fixed cost across the units produced.

questions.q: TFC is $240 and output is 12 units. AFC is:
TVC is $360 at 18 units of output. AVC is:
TC is $600 at 20 units. ATC is:
At 10 units, AFC is $8 and AVC is $22. ATC is:
questions.feedback: ATC = AFC + AVC = $8 + $22.

questions.q: A firm’s TFC is unchanged while output doubles. What happens to AFC?
options: It doubles
It stays unchanged
It becomes equal to TFC
It is cut in half
questions.feedback: AFC = TFC/Q, so doubling Q with the same TFC halves AFC.

questions.q: At 25 units, ATC is $18 and AFC is $4. AVC is:
questions.feedback: AVC = ATC − AFC = $18 − $4.

questions.q: A firm has TFC = $100, TVC = $300, and Q = 20. Which pair is correct?
options: AVC = $5 and ATC = $15
AVC = $15 and ATC = $20
AVC = $20 and ATC = $15
AFC = $15 and ATC = $20

questions.q: At Q = 40, ATC is $25 and AFC is $5. If TFC is unchanged, what is TVC at this output?
AFC falls from $12 to $8 while TFC remains $240. Output must have changed from:
options: 30 units to 20 units
12 units to 8 units
20 units to 24 units
20 units to 30 units
questions.feedback: Q = TFC/AFC, so output rises from 240/12 = 20 to 240/8 = 30.

questions.q: At Q = 50, TC is $1,400 and TFC is $400. Which average-cost values are correct?
options: AFC = $20 and AVC = $8
AFC = $28 and ATC = $8
AVC = $20 and ATC = $28
AVC = $28 and ATC = $20
questions.feedback: TVC = $1,000; AVC = $20, AFC = $8, and ATC = $28.

questions.q: A firm’s AVC is $16 at 30 units and its AFC is $6. If output rises and AFC falls to $4 while AVC stays $16, ATC becomes:
questions.feedback: ATC = AVC + AFC = $16 + $4.

questions.q: A learner divides output by TFC to calculate AFC. What is the repair?
options: AFC = TFC/Q
AFC = Q/TFC
AFC = TVC/Q
AFC = ΔTC/ΔQ
questions.feedback: Average fixed cost is fixed cost per unit of output.

questions.q: A learner calculates AVC using TC/Q. What is the repair?
options: AVC = TC/Q
AVC = TFC/Q
AVC = ΔTVC/Q
AVC = TVC/Q
questions.feedback: TC/Q is ATC; AVC uses total variable cost only.

questions.q: A learner says ATC = AVC − AFC. What is the repair?
options: ATC = MC + AFC
ATC = TC − Q
ATC = AVC + AFC
ATC = AFC − AVC
questions.feedback: Average total cost contains both average variable and average fixed cost.

questions.q: A learner says AFC eventually rises because “all U-shaped costs rise.” What is the repair?
options: AFC rises whenever MC rises
AFC keeps falling as fixed cost is spread over more output
AFC is U-shaped like AVC
AFC equals MC at its minimum
questions.feedback: AFC is not U-shaped in the standard model; it declines as quantity increases.

questions.q: At Q = 10, AFC = $6 and AVC = $14. A learner reports ATC = $8. What is the repair?
options: ATC is $20
ATC is $8
ATC is $14
ATC is $60
questions.feedback: ATC = AFC + AVC = $6 + $14.

questions.q: How does the fixed-cost concept connect to the downward slope of AFC?
options: TFC falls automatically as output rises
Variable cost is spread across fewer units
AFC is determined by marginal product only
The same TFC is spread across more units as output rises
questions.feedback: AFC falls because the numerator stays fixed while the denominator grows.

questions.q: How can rising average product of labor affect AVC when the wage is constant?
options: It must raise AVC because output is higher
It leaves every average cost unchanged
It tends to lower AVC because each worker produces more output per dollar of wage cost
It raises AFC only
questions.feedback: Higher output per worker reduces variable labor cost per unit.

questions.q: How does the identity TC = TFC + TVC connect to ATC?
options: ATC excludes fixed cost
Dividing by Q gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by Q gives ATC = MC + AVC
ATC equals TC minus output
questions.feedback: The average-cost identity follows directly from the total-cost identity.

questions.q: Why can ATC fall even when AVC is flat?
options: Falling AFC can pull ATC downward
ATC never includes fixed cost
MC must be zero
TVC must be falling
questions.feedback: Because ATC = AVC + AFC, a declining fixed-cost component can reduce ATC.

questions.q: Why is AVC often more relevant than AFC for understanding the cost of current production activity?
options: AFC determines how much extra output one worker adds
AVC includes all sunk costs
AFC changes directly with every unit produced
AVC reflects variable resources used to produce the current output
questions.feedback: Variable cost is tied to inputs adjusted as production changes.

questions.q: How does a below-average marginal cost affect ATC?
options: It leaves ATC unchanged by definition
It makes AFC rise
It pulls ATC downward
It pushes ATC upward
questions.feedback: The marginal-versus-average rule applies to costs just as it does to other averages.

questions.q: Marginal cost measures:
options: Revenue minus variable cost
The change in total cost from producing additional output
Total cost per unit of output
Fixed cost per unit
questions.feedback: MC is the change in cost associated with a change in output.

questions.q: If output rises by 1 unit and total cost rises by $18, marginal cost of that unit is:
options: Cannot be determined
questions.feedback: With a one-unit output change, MC equals the increase in total cost.

questions.q: A pure increase in total fixed cost has what direct effect on marginal cost?
options: Raises MC by the full fixed-cost increase
Lowers MC to zero
Makes MC equal AFC
No effect
questions.feedback: A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.

questions.q: With a constant wage, when marginal product of labor rises, marginal cost generally:
options: Stays fixed
Becomes equal to TFC
Falls
Rises
questions.feedback: More output from an additional worker lowers labor cost per extra unit.

questions.q: With a constant wage, diminishing marginal product eventually causes marginal cost to:
options: Become negative
Rise
Fall continuously
Remain constant
questions.feedback: When additional labor adds less output, each extra unit becomes more costly to produce.

questions.q: If TVC rises from $200 to $236 when output rises from 10 to 12 units, MC over that interval is:
options: $18 per unit
$36 per unit
$118 per unit
$2 per unit

questions.q: Marginal cost can be calculated from changes in TC or TVC because:
options: TVC is always equal to TC
AFC is constant
TC excludes fixed cost
TFC does not change with output
questions.feedback: Since fixed cost is unchanged, ΔTC = ΔTVC when output changes.

questions.q: If one additional worker costs $120 and adds 8 units of output, the labor-cost contribution to MC is:
options: $120 per unit
$960 per unit
$15 per unit
$8 per unit
questions.feedback: With a constant wage, $120/8 = $15 of labor cost per additional unit.

questions.q: Total cost rises from $540 to $600 as output rises from 20 to 24 units. Marginal cost over the interval is:
options: $135 per unit
$15 per unit
$60 per unit
$25 per unit

questions.q: A worker costs $180 per shift. The worker’s marginal product falls from 12 units to 9 units as employment expands. Holding the wage constant, the implied labor cost per marginal unit changes from:
questions.feedback: W/MP rises from 180/12 = 15 to 180/9 = 20 as marginal product falls.

questions.q: A $500 monthly license fee is imposed regardless of output. Which statement about MC is correct?
options: MC rises by $500 for every unit
MC falls because AFC rises
MC becomes equal to ATC
MC is unchanged because the fee does not vary with output
questions.feedback: A fixed fee shifts fixed and average total cost, not the incremental cost of output.

questions.q: A technology change lets each additional worker produce more output at the same wage. What happens to marginal cost, other things equal?
options: It is unchanged
It becomes a fixed cost
It falls
It rises
questions.feedback: Higher marginal product means the same labor expense creates more additional output.

questions.q: TVC is $300 at 15 units and $390 at 20 units. What is MC between these outputs?
A learner calculates MC as TC/Q. What is the repair?
options: MC = ΔTC/ΔQ
MC = TC/Q
MC = TFC/Q
MC = TVC/Q
questions.feedback: TC/Q is average total cost; marginal cost uses changes.

questions.q: A learner says a higher fixed property tax must raise MC. What is the repair?
options: Every fixed-cost increase raises MC one-for-one
MC equals AFC after a tax
Fixed costs are part of TVC
A pure fixed-cost increase does not change MC
questions.feedback: MC depends on changes in cost as output changes, and a fixed amount is present at every output.

questions.q: A learner says falling marginal product causes MC to fall. What is the repair?
options: Marginal product and MC always move together
Marginal product affects fixed cost only
With a constant input price, falling marginal product raises MC
Falling marginal product lowers both MC and AVC automatically
questions.feedback: Less extra output from the same variable-input expense raises cost per additional unit.

questions.q: TC rises by $50 when output rises by 5 units, but a learner reports MC = $50. What is the repair?
options: MC cannot use total cost
MC is $10 per unit
MC is $55 per unit
MC is $250 per unit
questions.feedback: Divide the cost change by the output change: $50/5 = $10.

questions.q: A worker costs $100 and adds 10 units. A learner reports MC from labor as $100 per unit. What is the repair?
options: The labor cost per marginal unit is $10
The labor cost per marginal unit is $100
Marginal product should be added to the wage
The worker’s wage is a fixed cost
questions.feedback: Divide the worker’s cost by the worker’s marginal product: $100/10 = $10 per unit.

questions.q: ATC falls up to Q = 40 and rises beyond Q = 40. At Q = 40, which relationship should hold?
options: MC is below AVC
AFC equals ATC
MC is at its maximum
MC equals ATC
questions.feedback: Marginal cost intersects average total cost at ATC’s minimum.

questions.q: At the output where AVC reaches its minimum, which statement is correct?
options: ATC equals AFC
MC must be below AVC
MC equals AVC
MC equals AFC
questions.feedback: The marginal-cost curve passes through average variable cost at AVC’s minimum.

questions.q: A higher fixed license fee shifts which short-run average-cost curves upward?
options: AVC only
AFC and ATC
AVC and MC
MC only
questions.feedback: A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.

questions.q: A higher wage for production workers shifts which curves upward, other things equal?
options: AVC, ATC, and MC
AFC only
AFC and ATC only
TFC only
questions.feedback: A production wage is a variable cost and affects the cost of additional output.

questions.q: MC is below AVC but rising. What must AVC be doing at that output?
options: Rising
At its maximum
Equal to AFC
Falling
questions.feedback: A marginal below the average pulls the average downward even if the marginal itself is rising.

questions.q: MC is above ATC. What must be happening to ATC?
options: ATC is constant
ATC equals AVC
ATC is rising
ATC is falling
questions.feedback: A marginal above the average pulls the average upward.

questions.q: A technology improvement reduces the variable input needed at every output. Which short-run curves should generally shift downward?
options: TFC and AFC only
AVC, ATC, and MC
AFC only
AFC and ATC only
questions.feedback: Lower variable resource requirements reduce variable cost per unit and marginal cost.

questions.q: At a given output, ATC is $30 and AVC is $24. The vertical gap between those curves is:
questions.feedback: The ATC–AVC gap equals AFC.

questions.q: A learner says MC must be falling whenever ATC is falling. What is the repair?
options: ATC can fall only if MC is zero
MC and ATC always have the same slope
ATC falls only when AFC rises
MC can be rising while ATC is still falling, as long as MC remains below ATC
questions.feedback: The direction of the average depends on whether the marginal is above or below it, not on whether the marginal is itself rising.

questions.q: A learner says a higher fixed insurance premium shifts AVC and MC upward. What is the repair?
options: All short-run curves shift by the same amount
A fixed-cost increase lowers ATC
A pure fixed-cost increase shifts AFC and ATC, not AVC or MC
A fixed-cost increase shifts only MC
questions.feedback: Fixed cost does not change the variable cost of current output or the incremental cost of another unit.

questions.q: A sunk cost is a cost that:
options: Exists only when economic profit is negative
Has already been incurred and cannot be recovered
Always varies with current output
Can always be avoided by shutting down today
questions.feedback: A sunk cost is unrecoverable and should not be changed by the current decision.

questions.q: An avoidable cost is a cost that:
options: Can be eliminated by choosing a particular alternative
Has already been paid and cannot be recovered
Must be fixed in every time period
Is excluded from economic cost
questions.feedback: Avoidable costs differ across the alternatives being considered.

questions.q: A nonrefundable $2,000 design fee was paid last month. For today’s continue-or-cancel decision, the fee is:
options: Avoidable
Marginal revenue
An implicit future cost
Sunk
questions.feedback: The payment cannot be recovered regardless of the current choice.

questions.q: A monthly service contract can be canceled before next month with no penalty. Next month’s payment is:
options: An implicit cost only
A past fixed cost
Avoidable
Sunk
questions.feedback: A future cost that disappears under one option is relevant to the decision.

questions.q: A theater paid $5,000 for an advertising campaign that cannot be refunded. It is deciding whether to hold an event tomorrow. How should the $5,000 enter the decision?
options: It should determine the ticket price
It should be ignored because it is sunk
It should be charged again to tomorrow’s event
It should be treated as marginal cost of each ticket
questions.feedback: The advertising payment is unrecoverable and identical under either current choice.

questions.q: A firm can cancel a future equipment rental and save $3,000 if it stops a project. The $3,000 is:
options: An avoidable cost relevant to the stop-or-continue choice
A sunk cost because equipment is fixed
An implicit cost with no monetary payment
Irrelevant because it is a fixed monthly amount
questions.feedback: Future fixed commitments can be avoidable if the decision eliminates them.

questions.q: A company spent $40,000 developing software that now has no resale value. A new update would cost $8,000 and generate an expected $11,000 benefit. Ignoring other effects, what should the firm do?
options: Reject the update because total spending would become $48,000
Reject the update because sunk costs must be recovered first
Buy the update only if the original $40,000 is refunded
Buy the update because the $40,000 is sunk and the incremental benefit exceeds the incremental cost
questions.feedback: The current decision compares the $11,000 additional benefit with the $8,000 additional cost.

questions.q: A store’s current lease payment is nonrefundable, but the lease ends this month. The owner is deciding whether to renew for another year. Which cost is relevant?
options: Both payments are sunk
Neither payment because rent is fixed
The future renewal payment
The current nonrefundable payment
questions.feedback: The current payment is sunk; the future renewal is avoidable and differs across options.

questions.q: A firm owns a specialized machine with no resale value. Its original purchase price is irrelevant to whether to use it for a new order because the purchase price is:
options: Marginal revenue
Sunk
Variable
Avoidable
questions.feedback: An unrecoverable past expenditure does not change across the current alternatives.

questions.q: A firm has already paid a nonrefundable $6,000 permit fee. Completing a project requires $14,000 more and will generate $17,000 in additional revenue. What is the correct decision logic?
options: Complete the project because the relevant incremental gain is $3,000
Cancel because total cost is $20,000
Cancel because the permit fee must be recovered
Complete only if revenue exceeds $23,000
questions.feedback: The sunk permit is irrelevant; compare $17,000 additional revenue with $14,000 avoidable completion cost.

questions.q: A plant pays $10,000 per month on a contract. If it closes now, $7,000 can be canceled but $3,000 must still be paid. For the close-or-operate choice, how much of the monthly contract is avoidable?
questions.feedback: Only the portion that disappears when the plant closes is avoidable.

questions.q: A publisher spent $25,000 editing a book. It can print the book for an additional $12,000 and expects $15,000 in additional sales. Which statement is correct?
options: The editing cost should be allocated to each future copy before deciding
The firm must recover all $25,000 before printing
Printing adds $3,000 to profit relative to not printing, because the editing cost is sunk
Printing loses $22,000 because total cost is $37,000
questions.feedback: The current decision compares the $15,000 incremental revenue with the $12,000 avoidable printing cost.

questions.q: A fixed annual license can be surrendered halfway through the year for a $4,000 refund. For a midyear shutdown decision, which amount is relevant?
options: Only variable labor cost can be relevant
$4,000 because shutting down recovers it
$0 because every fixed cost is sunk
The full original license price regardless of refund
questions.feedback: The recoverable amount differs across choices and is therefore avoidable rather than sunk.

questions.q: A learner says, “Fixed cost and sunk cost mean the same thing.” What is the repair?
options: A fixed cost can be avoidable in a future decision; a sunk cost is unrecoverable
Every sunk cost varies with output
Every fixed cost has already been paid forever
Sunk costs are always implicit
questions.feedback: Fixed describes how cost behaves with current output; sunk describes whether it can be recovered.

questions.q: A learner includes a nonrefundable past payment when comparing two current options that both leave the payment unchanged. What is the repair?
options: Double the payment to reflect risk
Treat it as marginal cost
Convert it into future revenue
Ignore the payment because it is sunk and identical across the options
questions.feedback: Only costs and benefits that differ across current alternatives should affect the choice.

questions.q: A learner calls a cancelable future lease payment sunk because the lease is a fixed cost. What is the repair?
options: Only variable costs can be avoided
A lease payment is always implicit
The future payment is avoidable if canceling the lease eliminates it
All fixed costs are sunk
questions.feedback: A cost can be fixed with respect to output yet avoidable with respect to a future decision.

questions.q: How does the sunk-cost rule connect to marginal analysis?
options: Both rules say fixed costs are always irrelevant
Both focus the current choice on additional costs and benefits that change across alternatives
Marginal analysis requires adding all past costs
Sunk cost is another term for marginal cost
questions.feedback: Past unrecoverable costs do not change the marginal consequences of the current decision.

questions.q: How can a cost be fixed with respect to current output but still relevant to a future decision?
options: It may be avoidable if choosing a different plan eliminates the future payment
Every fixed cost is permanently sunk
Fixed costs always change one-for-one with output
Future fixed costs are excluded from economic cost
questions.feedback: Cost behavior with output and recoverability across decisions are different classifications.

questions.q: Why is “recovering what we already spent” a poor reason by itself to continue a project?
options: Past spending becomes revenue if the project continues
Sunk cost always raises marginal benefit
A project must continue until accounting profit is positive
Past unrecoverable spending is unchanged by the current choice, so the decision should compare future incremental benefits and costs
questions.feedback: The relevant comparison is forward-looking, not an attempt to reverse an unrecoverable past payment.

questions.q: Long-run average cost shows the lowest attainable average cost when:
options: Output must remain constant
Only labor can change
All inputs can be varied
At least one input is fixed
questions.feedback: The long run allows the firm to choose among plant sizes and adjust all inputs.

questions.q: LRAC falls from $28 per unit to $21 per unit as a firm expands its long-run output. This pattern indicates:
options: Diminishing marginal product from a fixed plant
Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Constant returns to scale
questions.feedback: Falling long-run average cost as scale expands indicates economies of scale.

questions.q: A very large firm becomes harder to coordinate, and its long-run cost per unit rises as it expands further. This is:
options: Diseconomies of scale
Economies of scale
Constant returns to scale
A fall in total product caused by one fixed input
questions.feedback: Rising unit cost at greater scale is diseconomies of scale; coordination problems are a common source.

questions.q: The LRAC curve is often described as an envelope because it:
options: Adds all short-run fixed costs together
Shows the highest ATC at every output
Is identical to one short-run ATC curve
Traces the lowest attainable ATC across available plant sizes
questions.feedback: In the long run, the firm can choose the least-cost plant for each output level.

questions.q: Which is a common source of economies of scale?
options: Management becoming harder to coordinate
A fall in marginal product caused by one fixed input
Greater specialization as the firm expands
A fixed input becoming more crowded
questions.feedback: Larger scale can support specialization of labor and capital that lowers average cost.

questions.q: Which is a common source of diseconomies of scale?
options: Bulk purchasing discounts
Coordination and communication problems in a very large organization
Spreading fixed cost over more units only
Workers specializing in narrower tasks
questions.feedback: Large scale can raise organizational and coordination costs per unit.

questions.q: Why can a firm choose a different plant size in long-run cost analysis?
options: All inputs are variable in the long run
Plant size is always variable in the short run
Fixed cost is zero at every output
Marginal cost determines plant size automatically
questions.feedback: The long run is defined by enough time to adjust all inputs, including plant capacity.

questions.q: A distribution network uses 40% more labor, buildings, and equipment but can handle 60% more shipments. This pattern is consistent with:
options: Diseconomies of scale
Constant returns to scale
A fixed short-run production function
Economies of scale
questions.feedback: Output expands more than proportionally to the expansion of all inputs.

questions.q: A company expands every input by 25%, but output increases by only 10%. Which scale result does this suggest?
options: Constant returns to scale
A reduction in total cost
Diseconomies of scale
Economies of scale
questions.feedback: Output rises less than proportionally to the increase in all inputs.

questions.q: Plant A has ATC $18 at 500 units and Plant B has ATC $15 at 500 units. If both plants are feasible in the long run, LRAC at 500 units cannot exceed:
questions.feedback: The firm can choose the lower-cost plant, so the long-run attainable average cost is at most $15.

questions.q: LRAC falls from $24 to $18 as output rises from 2,000 to 4,000 units. The firm is operating in a range of:
options: Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Constant returns to scale
Negative marginal product
questions.feedback: Average cost is falling as the scale of production expands.

questions.q: LRAC rises from $14 to $17 as output rises from 8,000 to 10,000 units. The firm is experiencing:
options: Economies of scale
Constant returns to scale
Falling total cost
Diseconomies of scale
questions.feedback: Rising long-run average cost with greater scale indicates diseconomies of scale.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes LRAC from a single SRATC curve?
options: LRAC is total cost rather than average cost
SRATC always lies below LRAC
LRAC reflects the least-cost plant choice at each output; a SRATC holds plant size fixed
LRAC holds all inputs fixed while SRATC varies all inputs
questions.feedback: Long-run cost allows plant adjustment; a particular short-run curve corresponds to a given plant.

questions.q: A larger factory permits dedicated machinery and specialized teams that reduce unit cost. This is an example of:
options: A sunk-cost effect
Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Diminishing marginal product from a fixed plant
questions.feedback: Specialization and indivisible technologies can lower LRAC as scale expands.

questions.q: At Q = 1,000 the lowest ATC among three plants is $22; at Q = 2,000 it is $17; at Q = 3,000 it is $19. Which sequence best describes LRAC over these outputs?
options: It falls and then rises
It rises and then falls
It is constant
It must equal the ATC of the smallest plant
questions.feedback: LRAC takes the lowest attainable ATC at each output, producing $22, $17, then $19.

questions.q: A firm increases every input by 50%, while output rises by 80%. Holding input prices constant, what should happen to average cost?
options: Average cost should rise
Average cost must remain unchanged
Average cost becomes fixed cost only
Average cost should fall
questions.feedback: Output rises more than proportionally to total input use, spreading cost over a larger proportional output increase.

questions.q: A manager blames rising LRAC at very large scale on “diminishing marginal product of labor.” What is the best correction?
options: Diseconomies require total product to fall
Diminishing marginal product and diseconomies are identical definitions
Diseconomies of scale are a long-run phenomenon involving changes in all inputs, not crowding one variable input against fixed inputs
The explanation is correct because the long run always has fixed capital
questions.feedback: Diminishing marginal product is a short-run concept; diseconomies concern scale when all inputs can vary.

questions.q: A learner treats LRAC as the ATC curve of one fixed plant. What is the repair?
options: LRAC is total variable cost per unit only
LRAC reflects the lowest attainable ATC across alternative plant sizes
LRAC is the same as AFC
LRAC fixes every input forever
questions.feedback: The long run permits plant adjustment, so LRAC summarizes least-cost choices across plants.

questions.q: A learner says economies of scale mean total cost must fall as output rises. What is the repair?
options: Economies of scale mean average cost falls; total cost can still rise
Economies mean output falls
Economies mean fixed cost becomes zero
Economies require marginal product to be negative
questions.feedback: The concept concerns cost per unit, not necessarily the level of total cost.

questions.q: A learner says diseconomies of scale begin when marginal product first falls in the short run. What is the repair?
options: Diseconomies and diminishing marginal product are the same event
Diseconomies require one input to remain fixed
Diseconomies mean LRAC is falling
Diseconomies concern long-run expansion of all inputs and rising LRAC
questions.feedback: The two concepts refer to different horizons and different input adjustments.

questions.q: A learner reads a downward-sloping LRAC segment as diseconomies of scale. What is the repair?
options: LRAC slope says nothing about scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment requires negative output
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents economies of scale
A downward-sloping LRAC segment represents constant returns
questions.feedback: Falling long-run average cost as output expands is economies of scale.

questions.q: A learner says rising LRAC means output itself must be falling. What is the repair?
options: Rising LRAC means total cost is falling
LRAC can rise while output expands; the issue is rising cost per unit at larger scale
Rising LRAC requires zero output
Output and LRAC always move in opposite directions
questions.feedback: Diseconomies describe a higher average cost at greater output, not a fall in output.

questions.q: How does specialization connect to economies of scale?
options: A larger scale can support specialized workers or capital that lowers cost per unit
Specialization always creates diminishing marginal product
Specialization raises fixed cost per unit forever
Specialization eliminates opportunity cost
questions.feedback: Scale can make specialized tasks and equipment economical, lowering LRAC over a range.

questions.q: How do coordination problems connect organizational size to diseconomies of scale?
options: Coordination problems reduce all input prices
They guarantee constant returns to scale
They turn fixed cost into sunk cost
Communication and management complexity can raise cost per unit as the organization grows
questions.feedback: Very large scale can create managerial inefficiencies that push LRAC upward.

questions.q: How does the short-run/long-run distinction connect SRATC curves to LRAC?
options: SRATC includes implicit cost but LRAC does not
The curves differ only because of revenue
Each SRATC holds a plant size fixed, while LRAC allows the firm to choose the least-cost plant for each output
LRAC fixes plant size while SRATC changes every input
questions.feedback: Long-run flexibility over plant size is what lets LRAC trace the least-cost envelope.

questions.q: How is economies of scale different from spreading a fixed short-run cost over more units?
options: Falling AFC is a long-run scale effect only
Economies of scale is a long-run change in cost per unit when all inputs can vary; falling AFC is a short-run arithmetic effect
They are identical concepts
Economies of scale requires one input to remain fixed
questions.feedback: Both can lower average cost, but they arise from different mechanisms and horizons.

questions.q: How can productivity improvements affect long-run average cost?
options: If the same inputs can produce more output, attainable cost per unit can fall
Higher productivity necessarily raises LRAC
Productivity affects revenue but never cost
Productivity makes all costs sunk
questions.feedback: More output from a given bundle of resources can lower the cost required per unit.

questions.q: Minimum efficient scale is the:
options: Largest output the firm can physically produce
Output where total cost is lowest
First output where marginal product is positive
Smallest output at which minimum LRAC is attained
questions.feedback: MES marks the first output level that reaches the minimum long-run average cost.

questions.q: A flat LRAC over a range of output is associated with:
options: Diseconomies of scale throughout the range
Diminishing marginal product only
Constant returns to scale
Economies of scale throughout the range
questions.feedback: A flat long-run average cost means proportional expansion does not change cost per unit.

questions.q: If LRAC first reaches its minimum at 5,000 units and remains flat until 8,000, MES is:
options: 13,000 units
5,000 units
8,000 units
6,500 units
questions.feedback: MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC.

questions.q: With constant returns to scale, doubling all inputs tends to:
options: Double output
More than double output
Increase output by less than double
Force output to remain unchanged
questions.feedback: Constant returns means output changes in the same proportion as all inputs.

options: 5,000 units
6,000 units
3,000 units
4,000 units
questions.feedback: The minimum LRAC is $12, first reached at 4,000 units.

questions.q: A firm increases all inputs by 25% and output also rises by 25%. This is consistent with:
options: Diseconomies of scale
Diminishing marginal product caused by fixed capital
Constant returns to scale
Economies of scale
questions.feedback: Output changes in the same proportion as all inputs.

questions.q: A firm’s LRAC reaches a flat minimum from 10,000 to 14,000 units. Which output is the minimum efficient scale?
questions.feedback: MES is the first output on the minimum-cost range.

questions.q: LRAC is $16 at both 20,000 and 30,000 units, and the curve is flat between them. Over that range the firm experiences:
options: Constant returns to scale
Economies of scale
Diseconomies of scale
Negative returns to labor
questions.feedback: An unchanged long-run cost per unit over a range is consistent with constant returns to scale.

questions.q: Why is the largest output on a flat minimum-LRAC segment not the MES?
options: MES is always the midpoint of the flat segment
MES is the output with highest total cost
MES requires LRAC to begin rising
MES is defined as the smallest output that attains minimum LRAC
questions.feedback: Larger outputs may also be efficient, but MES identifies the minimum scale needed to achieve the lowest unit cost.

questions.q: LRAC values are $22 at Q=1, $18 at Q=2, $15 at Q=3, $15 at Q=4, and $17 at Q=5. If quantities are thousands of units, which statement is correct?
options: MES is 5 thousand units because LRAC rises there
MES is 2 thousand units because LRAC is already falling
MES is 3 thousand units and constant returns hold from 3 to 4 thousand
MES is 4 thousand units because it is the largest minimum-cost output
questions.feedback: The minimum $15 first appears at 3 and remains unchanged through 4.

questions.q: A firm triples every input and output also triples. If input prices are unchanged, what happens to LRAC?
options: It must rise
It remains unchanged
It falls to one-third
It triples
questions.feedback: Proportional output and input expansion implies constant returns to scale and unchanged long-run unit cost.

questions.q: A firm can produce 6,000 units at LRAC $20, 8,000 at $16, 10,000 at $16, and 12,000 at $18. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: MES is 8,000 units; 8,000–10,000 is a minimum-cost range
MES is 10,000 units because output is larger
MES is 12,000 units because LRAC turns upward there
There is no MES because two outputs share the minimum
questions.feedback: MES is the smallest output attaining the minimum $16 LRAC.

questions.q: A learner chooses the largest output on a flat minimum-LRAC segment as MES. What is the repair?
options: MES is always the largest efficient output
MES is where LRAC first begins to fall
MES is where total cost is smallest
MES is the smallest output that attains the minimum LRAC
questions.feedback: The definition focuses on the minimum scale required to achieve the lowest long-run unit cost.

questions.q: A learner says a flat LRAC means output is not changing. What is the repair?
options: Flat LRAC means economies of scale
Flat LRAC means fixed cost is constant in the short run
Output can rise while LRAC stays constant; that range reflects constant returns to scale
Flat LRAC means output must be zero
questions.feedback: Constant returns refers to proportional changes in all inputs and output, leaving long-run cost per unit unchanged.

questions.q: How does MES build on the idea of economies of scale?
options: MES is the largest feasible plant regardless of cost
MES marks the smallest output at which the firm has exhausted the available LRAC reductions
MES is where diseconomies first begin at zero output
MES measures short-run AFC
questions.feedback: Before MES, additional scale can still lower long-run average cost; at MES the minimum has been reached.

questions.q: How does constant returns to scale differ from short-run diminishing marginal product?
options: Constant returns is a long-run proportional change in all inputs; diminishing marginal product varies one input with others fixed
They are identical concepts
Constant returns requires a fixed plant
Diminishing marginal product requires all inputs to change proportionally
questions.feedback: The concepts apply to different production experiments and time horizons.

questions.q: Why can MES matter when comparing efficient firm scale with the size of a market?
options: It determines consumer demand directly
It fixes the market price by law
It measures accounting profit rather than cost
It indicates the minimum output needed to achieve the lowest available long-run unit cost
questions.feedback: MES summarizes how much output a firm must reach before it captures all available scale economies.
